nodes.label: Armenian exodus to Cilicia
nodes.full: After the fall of Ani in 1064, the Armenian nobles and peoples left the Armenian plateau in large numbers and moved to Cappadocia, the Taurus and Cilicia, as soldiers of the Byzantines and as independent chiefs. The Cilician kingdom was the work of this diaspora.
nodes.src: Matthew of Edessa; Samuel of Ani; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Ruben and the Taurus lords
nodes.full: After the fall of the Armenian kingdoms and the Turkish conquest of the plateau, Armenian nobles took refuge in the Taurus mountains of Cilicia. Ruben, said to be a kinsman of the last Bagratid king, built a principality around Vahka (Feke) from about 1080, and his sons Constantine and Thoros ruled from the fortresses of Vahka and Partzerpert. They dealt with Byzantines, Crusaders and Turks as occasion demanded.
nodes.src: Matthew of Edessa; Samuel of Ani; Sempad the Constable's Chronicle; Claude Mutafian, L'Arménie du Levant (2012).

nodes.label: Lords of Lampron
nodes.full: The Hethumids of Lampron, rivals of the Rubenids, held the fortress of Lampron in the Taurus above Tarsus and had long ruled the Cilician Gates. Their house, with its learned archbishops, castles and its alliance with the Byzantines, gave the kingdom its second dynasty by the marriage of Hethum to Zabel.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Nerses of Lambron; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Leo I, Thoros II
nodes.full: Leo I took Mopsuestia, Adana and Tarsus from the Byzantines and was captured by John II Komnenos in 1137, dying in captivity. His son Thoros II escaped from Constantinople in 1143, regained the family lands, and held them against Manuel I, who invaded in 1158. He raided Cyprus with Reynald of Châtillon in 1156.
nodes.src: Niketas Choniates; John Kinnamos; Michael the Syrian; Sempad's Chronicle.

nodes.label: John II in Cilicia
nodes.full: In 1137 John II Komnenos marched into Cilicia, took Tarsus, Adana, Mopsuestia and Anazarbus, captured Leo I and his sons at Vahka and sent them to Constantinople. The Byzantines restored their rule over the plain for a generation, though the mountain families remained.
nodes.src: Niketas Choniates 1; John Kinnamos 1; Sempad's Chronicle; Michael the Syrian.

nodes.label: Manuel I and Thoros II
nodes.full: Thoros II, who had raided the Byzantines' Cyprus with Reynald of Châtillon in 1156, was driven into the hills by Manuel I Komnenos's army in 1158. Manuel made him a vassal of the empire and recovered the plain. The Armenian prince's alliance with Nur al-Din in the following years contained the Franks.
nodes.src: John Kinnamos 4; Niketas Choniates 3; William of Tyre 18.

nodes.label: Hromgla and Shnorhali
nodes.full: Catholicos Gregory III gave the Armenian Church a seat at the Euphrates fortress of Hromgla in 1149. Under Nerses IV Shnorhali, 'the Graceful' (1166–1173), it was a centre of theology, hymns and letters to Greek and Latin churchmen seeking union. The see stayed there till 1292.
nodes.src: Nerses Shnorhali, Encyclical, Letters to Manuel, Jesus the Son; Der Nersessian 1962.

nodes.label: Hymns and khaz
nodes.full: Nerses Shnorhali wrote sharakans (hymns), poetry and an elegy on the fall of Edessa. The Armenian church kept its hymns in a notation of khaz signs, which, from the twelfth century, marked melodic motion and are still only partly understood. Cilician manuscripts are the main source for the classic chant.
nodes.src: Nerses Shnorhali, Hymns; Nicolas Lerner on khaz notation; Der Nersessian 1962.

nodes.label: Nerses of Lambron
nodes.full: Nerses, archbishop of Tarsus and a member of the Lampron family, studied Greek, Latin and Syriac, translated the Rule of Saint Benedict and Latin texts into Armenian and wrote commentaries on the liturgy. His speech at the Council of Hromgla in 1179 was a plea for a union based on respect for different customs.
nodes.src: Nerses Lambronatsi, Explanation of the Mass; Speech at the Council of Hromgla (1179).

nodes.label: Leo the Magnificent
nodes.full: Leo II, who became prince in 1187 and king in 1198, brought together the Armenian lands of Cilicia, took the Frankish title and a crown from the Emperor Henry VI and the Pope, and made Sis a capital. He fought the Seljuks, Bohemond III and IV of Antioch, the Templars and the Ayyubids and left to his daughter a rich kingdom.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Smbat's Chronicle; Ibn al-Athir; Mutafian 2012; Sirarpie Der Nersessian, 'The Kingdom of Cilician Armenia', in Setton (ed.), A History of the Crusades vol. 2.

nodes.label: Death of Barbarossa
nodes.full: Leo II, then the Armenian prince, was to give the Third Crusade provisions and a guide, but the emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned in the river Saleph in June 1190, and his army split up. Leo's contacts with the German emperor led to his royal crown in 1198.
nodes.src: Historia de expeditione Friderici imperatoris; Ansbert; Arnold of Lübeck.

nodes.label: Coronation of 1198
nodes.full: In the Cathedral of St Sophia at Tarsus, Leo was anointed by the Catholicos Gregory VI and crowned by the representative of the emperor Henry VI, the chancellor Conrad of Hildesheim, who brought a crown. The Pope Celestine III had recognised the title. The coronation made him King of All Armenia and gave the Cilician state a new place in Christendom.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Der Nersessian 1962; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Antiochene succession
nodes.full: When Bohemond III of Antioch died, his grandson Raymond-Ruben, Leo's protégé, claimed the principality against Bohemond IV, and Leo fought for him, with Templars, Hospitallers and Seljuks all taking sides, until his death. Leo held Antioch for a time, but Bohemond IV prevailed.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Ibn al-Athir; Steven Runciman, A History of the Crusades vol. 3.

nodes.label: Privileges of Genoa and Venice
nodes.full: Leo II gave the Genoese and the Venetians privileges in his ports — quarters, exemption from duties, their own consuls and courts — in return for naval aid. Under his successors the privileges were confirmed. The Italian cities used Ayas as the base of their trade with Persia and the Mongol world.
nodes.src: Genoese privilege of 1201 (Liber iurium); Venetian pact of 1201; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Teutonic Knights
nodes.full: Leo II gave the Teutonic Order the castles of Amudain and Haruniye (Harunia) and a place at Sis, as a part of his policy of rewarding the military orders against the Templars, who were backing his rival at Antioch. It was one of the Order's first holdings in the East.
nodes.src: Teutonic Order charter of 1212 (Tabulae ordinis Theutonici); Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Latinised feudal order
nodes.full: The Armenian state adopted Frankish feudal titles and institutions: baron, constable, marshal, chancellor, bailli and the knights, along with Armenian noble families, the tanuters, and Latin Church ranks. Men dressed and fought in Frankish manner. The court was a blend of Armenian and Frankish usage, in Armenian, French and Latin.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Mutafian 2012; Jacques de Morgan, Histoire du peuple arménien.

nodes.label: Castles of Cilicia
nodes.full: The Armenian lords built, rebuilt and held a chain of castles on the Taurus crags and the coast — Lampron, Vahka, Sis, Anavarza, Yılan Kale ('Snake Castle'), Korykos's Sea Castle (1206) — with towers, curtains, cisterns and chapels. They mixed Byzantine, Armenian and Crusader military building into a style of their own.
nodes.src: Robert Edwards, The Fortifications of Armenian Cilicia (1987).

nodes.label: Ayas
nodes.full: Ayas on the Gulf of Alexandretta was the terminus of the overland route from Tabriz and Persia and the leading port of the Levant after Acre fell. Marco Polo went through it in 1271 and Pegolotti listed the customs and the conditions of its markets in his merchants' handbook of the 1340s. Genoese, Venetians and Pisans had their quarters.
nodes.src: Marco Polo, Travels 1; Francesco Pegolotti, Pratica della mercatura (c. 1340); Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Cilician plain
nodes.full: The fertile Cilician plain provided the state with grain, cotton, wine, olive oil and fruit, which the Italian traders exported to Cyprus and Italy. The plain, with its walled towns of Adana, Mopsuestia and Tarsus, was the kingdom's richest land, and its holding the object of every foreign campaign.
nodes.src: Pegolotti; Mutafian 2012; Hellenkemper and Hild 1990.

nodes.label: The tram
nodes.full: The kingdom minted a silver coin, the tram, with the king enthroned or on horseback and an Armenian legend, and a gold takavorin. The coin was used in trade with Italy and Cyprus and competed with the Venetian grosso. Its value was kept for much of the thirteenth century.
nodes.src: Paul Bedoukian, Coinage of Cilician Armenia (1962).

nodes.label: Zabel and Hethum I
nodes.full: Leo's daughter Zabel was crowned queen as a child. She was married to Philip of Antioch, who was deposed and died in prison in 1225, and then to Hethum, the son of the lord of Lampron, in 1226. Hethum ruled for forty-three years, submitted to the Mongols in 1244 and brought Cilicia under their protection.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Kirakos of Gandzak; Het'um of Korykos; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Queen Zabel
nodes.full: Zabel (Isabella), crowned as a child on Leo's death, was the object of a struggle between the barons and her guardians, abducted by one and forced into a marriage with Philip of Antioch, whom she did not love and who was removed. She co-ruled with Hethum, to whom she was married at twelve, until her death in 1252.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Kirakos of Gandzak; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Hethum at Karakorum
nodes.full: Hethum I travelled across Asia in 1254 and 1255 to meet the Great Khan Möngke, from whom he received a charter of protection for the Armenian church and lands, and an alliance against the Muslims. His brother Smbat had made the journey earlier. The Armenian kingdom became part of the Mongol system of vassals.
nodes.src: Kirakos of Gandzak; Het'um of Korykos, Flor des estoires; Jackson 2005.

nodes.label: Armenians with the Mongols
nodes.full: Hethum I, who had visited the Great Khan in 1254, joined Hulagu's army with his troops in 1259 and 1260, and took part in the capture of Aleppo and Damascus together with Bohemond VI of Antioch. After the Mongol defeat at Ain Jalut the Armenians paid for their loyalty.
nodes.src: Kirakos of Gandzak; Het'um of Korykos; Bar Hebraeus; Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West (2005).

nodes.label: Mari and Sis
nodes.full: Baybars sent an army into Cilicia in 1266, which defeated the Armenians at the Mari plain, killed Hethum's son Thoros and took the other son, Leo. The Mamluks sacked Sis, Adana and Ayas. Hethum had to give up the border castles and ransom his son at the price of Darbsak and Terbezak.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Furat; Baybars's chronicles; Sempad's Chronicle; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Smbat’s code
nodes.full: The Constable Smbat, brother of King Hethum, compiled a law code in 1265 on the basis of Mkhitar Gosh's Armenian code and the custom of Cilicia, with the influence of the Assizes of Antioch. It is the main source of the law of the kingdom and was later used in the Armenian colonies abroad.
nodes.src: Smbat Sparapet, Datastanagirk (ed. Aucher, Venice 1876); Assises d'Antioche (Armenian version).

nodes.label: Smbat’s Chronicle
nodes.full: Smbat the Constable, brother of Hethum I, wrote a Chronicle of his people from 951 to 1272 in Armenian, with the events of his own time from personal knowledge, including missions to the Mongols and the Seljuks. He is the best contemporary source for the kingdom.
nodes.src: Smbat Sparapet, Chronicle (trans. Robert Bedrosian, 2005).

nodes.label: Roslin’s Gospels
nodes.full: Toros Roslin, an illuminator in the scriptorium at Hromgla and at Sis, painted Gospel books for the Catholicos and the royal family — the Zeytun Gospels (1256), the Malatya Gospels (1268) and the Queen Keran Gospels — with architectural canon tables, rich colours and gold and a new naturalism from Byzantine, Latin and Islamic art.
nodes.src: Zeytun Gospels (Matenadaran 10450); Malatya Gospels (Jerusalem, Armenian Patriarchate MS 251); Sirarpie Der Nersessian, Armenian Art (1977); Helen Evans (ed.), Armenia: Art, Religion and Trade in the Middle Ages (2018).

nodes.label: Queen Keran
nodes.full: Keran, wife of Leo III and daughter of the lord of Lampron, was a patron of the arts who gave Toros Roslin's Gospels for her family. A miniature in her Gospel book shows the queen and her children in procession and Armenian court dress. It is a rare portrait of an Armenian queen.
nodes.src: Queen Keran Gospels (Jerusalem, Armenian Patriarchate MS 2563); Der Nersessian 1977.

nodes.label: Leo III to Leo IV
nodes.full: Leo III, his son Hethum II and their successors reigned in the shadow of Mamluk invasions and the Mongol alliance, with many dynastic murders. Hethum II became a Franciscan, abdicated more than once and was murdered with his young nephew Leo in 1307 at Anavarza by a Mongol general, and the Hethumid line died out with Oshin's son Leo in 1341.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Het'um of Korykos; Aytonus; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Fall of Hromgla
nodes.full: After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil took the Euphrates fortress of Hromgla, the seat of the Armenian Catholicos since 1149, after a siege of thirty-three days. The Catholicate moved to Sis. It was the last major Armenian holding east of the Taurus.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Furat; Abu'l-Fida; Sempad's Chronicle.

nodes.label: Councils of Sis and Adana
nodes.full: Hethum II and his nephew Oshin, anxious for Western aid, had the Council of Sis in 1307 accept Latin practices — the date of Christmas, the use of water in the chalice and the Roman creed — and the Council of Adana in 1316 pushed further. The Armenian clergy, strongly opposed, resisted them and the greater part of the Church of Greater Armenia rejected them.
nodes.src: Council of Sis canons (1307); Mutafian 2012; Sirarpie Der Nersessian 1962.

nodes.label: Het’um of Korykos
nodes.full: Het'um of Korykos, a nephew of the king who became a Premonstratensian canon in Cyprus, dictated in Poitiers in 1307 to Nicolas Falcon La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient, a description of the East, its history and the Mongols, with a plan for a crusade. It was widely read in Latin, French and English.
nodes.src: Het'um of Korykos, Flos historiarum terre orientis (RHC Arm. 2); Robert Bedrosian trans. (2004).

nodes.label: Last mainland Christian state
nodes.full: After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Armenian kingdom was the only Christian state left on the mainland of the Near East. It survived another eighty years as the objective of papal crusade plans and of Mamluk campaigns, and its fall in 1375 closed the crusader era on the mainland.
nodes.src: Het'um of Korykos; Mutafian 2012; Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 3.

nodes.label: Lusignan kings
nodes.full: When the Hethumid line ended, the barons elected Guy of Lusignan, Constantine II, from the royal house of Cyprus, in 1342. His Latin-minded successors Constantine III, IV and Leo V were hated by the Armenian nobility and the Armenian church. Sis fell to the Mamluks in 1375, and Leo V, the last king, was a prisoner and then an exile.
nodes.src: Mutafian 2012; Jean Richard, Le royaume latin de Jérusalem; Machaut, La Prise d'Alexandrie.

nodes.label: Lusignan marriages
nodes.full: The royal houses of Cyprus and Armenia were bound by marriages, beginning with that of Henry I of Cyprus to Stephanie, sister of Hethum I, in 1237, and by repeated mutual aid. When the Hethumid line ended in 1341, the Armenian barons offered the throne to Guy of Lusignan, a Cypriot. Armenia was in effect a part of the Lusignan world.
nodes.src: Sempad's Chronicle; Louis de Mas Latrie, Histoire de l'île de Chypre (1852–61).

nodes.label: Mamluk conquest
nodes.full: The Mamluks took Ayas in 1337 and, in 1359, Tarsus, Adana and Mopsuestia. In April 1375 Sis, the capital, fell after a siege, and King Leo V surrendered with his family. The last Armenian state in the Near East came to an end.
nodes.src: Al-Maqrizi; Ibn Taghribirdi; Mutafian 2012.

nodes.label: Leo V in exile
nodes.full: Leo V, taken to Cairo after the fall of Sis and held for six years, was freed in 1382 and travelled to Europe, to Spain, Avignon, Rome and the courts of France and England, seeking a crusade that never came. He died in Paris in 1393, a king without a kingdom.
nodes.src: Froissart, Chroniques 3; Mutafian 2012; Sirarpie Der Nersessian 1962.

nodes.label: Fall of Ani and the Seljuk invasion
nodes.full: Alp Arslan took Ani in 1064 and the Turkmen soon after overran the Armenian plateau, scattering the Armenian nobility.
nodes.src: background — see the Byzantine Anatolia 867–1071 folio (byzantine-anatolia-867-1071)

nodes.label: The fall of Acre
nodes.full: The Mamluks took Acre in 1291 and ended the Crusader states on the Syrian mainland, leaving Cilician Armenia as the one Christian state left.
nodes.src: background — see the Crusader States 1099–1291 folio (crusader-states-1099-1291)
